paragraphs: Our Sages compared the laws of washing the hands to the laws of purifying the waters of the sin-offering (mei chatat) and to the sanctification of hands and feet from the laver (kiyor) — since a change in appearance disqualifies those waters, so too with water for washing the hands one must be careful about this, as will be explained, please God. Even if the water changed by itself — for example, water that stood in vessels in the air for a long time and turned green — it is likewise disqualified. And even though many disagree and hold that water which changed by itself remains valid, since Maran [Rabbi Yosef Karo], whose rulings we have accepted, ruled that it is disqualified, that is our practice. However, if one has no other water and cannot obtain other water, he may wash with it, but should not recite the berachah with God's name and kingship — rather he should have the name and kingship in mind in his heart. Any water whose appearance changed and was disqualified, if it returned to its original state, returns to being valid.

clarification.explanation: Our Sages compared the laws of washing the hands to the laws of purifying the waters of the sin-offering and to the sanctification of hands and feet from the laver in the Temple. Just as a change of color disqualifies the water there, so too one must be careful about this in washing the hands. Even if the water changed color by itself — for example, water that stood for a long time in a vessel in the air and turned greenish — it too is disqualified for washing. Although there are opinions that disagree and validate water that changed by itself, since Maran (Rabbi Yosef Karo), whom we follow, ruled that it is disqualified — that is the practice. But if a person has no other water and cannot obtain any, he should wash his hands with it, but should not recite the berachah with God's name and kingship, but rather should have the words in mind in his heart. Water that was disqualified due to a change of color, if it returns to its original appearance, becomes valid for washing again.
takeaways: Water whose appearance changed, even by itself, is disqualified for washing the hands.
If there is no other water and none can be obtained, one washes with it without reciting the berachah aloud with God's name and kingship, but has it in mind in the heart.
Water that was disqualified and then returned to its original appearance is valid again.

paragraphs: Water into which dust or mud fell — even though it became turbid and its appearance changed — remains valid, because the growth [source] of water is amid dust and mud and that is its natural way, so this is not considered a change. Nevertheless, if it is so turbid that a dog cannot drink from it, it is disqualified.

clarification.explanation: Water into which dust or mud fell, becoming turbid and changing color, is still valid for washing the hands and the like. The reason is that water by nature exists together with dust and mud, so such a change is considered normal and does not disqualify it. But if the water becomes so turbid that even a dog cannot drink from it, then it is disqualified.
takeaways: Water that became dirtied with dust or mud and turned turbid remains valid as long as a dog could drink from it.
If the turbidity is so severe that even a dog would not drink it, the water is disqualified.

paragraphs: If work was done with the water — such as rinsing moldy or dirty vessels in it — it is disqualified; but if one rinsed clean, already-washed vessels in it, it remains valid. And if one soaked fruits, vegetables, or bread in it — even if he intended to soak them in one vessel and it fell into this one — it is disqualified, because once a person does with the water something he needs, it becomes like waste water (shofchin) destined to be poured out, and one may not wash hands with shofchin. Some say that even if he did not intend to soak anything at all, but bread or the like simply fell into the water by itself, it is likewise disqualified. And even though the language of Maran and the great halachic authorities does not imply this — rather it implies that whatever fell in by itself remains valid, since it was not made into shofchin — nevertheless, one should be concerned lechatchilah [ab initio] for the stricter view: if he has other water, he should not wash with this water; and if he has no other water, he should wash with it, but recite the berachah without God's name and kingship, and instead have the name and kingship in mind in his heart, since we hold that in a doubt about berachot we are lenient.

clarification.explanation: If work was done with the water, such as rinsing moldy or dirty vessels in it, the water is disqualified for washing the hands. But if clean, already-rinsed vessels were rinsed in it, the water remains valid. If fruits, vegetables, or bread were soaked in it — even if one intended to soak them in one vessel and the food fell by mistake into another — the water is disqualified, because once a person does something in the water that benefits him, the water is considered waste water destined to be poured out, and one does not wash hands with waste water. Some say that even if the food fell into the water entirely by itself without any intention, the water is disqualified. And although from the words of Maran the Shulchan Aruch and the great authorities it appears that if the food fell in by itself the water remains valid, since it was not turned into waste water, nevertheless one should, lechatchilah, be concerned for the stricter opinion. Therefore: if he has other water, he should not wash with this water. If he has no other water, he washes with it, but recites the berachah without God's name and kingship, only having the name and kingship in mind in his heart, since in a doubt about berachot we are lenient.
takeaways: If clean vessels were rinsed in the water, it remains valid for washing; if the vessels were dirty, the water is disqualified.
If food was soaked in the water (even if it fell in by mistake), the water is disqualified for washing.

If the food fell into the water by itself: lechatchilah one should be stringent and not wash with it, but if there is no other water, one washes and recites the berachah without God's name and kingship, only having it in mind in the heart.

paragraphs: Work disqualifies water only when it is drawn water (mayim she'uvin) — whether in vessels or in the ground — when the work was done in it and it is afterward taken up in a vessel to wash from it. But if work was done in the water of a mikveh or a spring while it was still attached [to its source], it is not disqualified; however, a change of appearance does disqualify it, even while attached. To what does this apply? To washing the hands. But to immerse one's hands in it, one may do so if it is valid for immersing the whole body — such as a spring, in which a change of appearance does not disqualify, or a mikveh whose water's appearance changed due to something insubstantial, such as the rinsing of baskets of olives and grapes, or into which colored water fell — as is written in Yoreh De'ah siman 201, and as mentioned in the Shulchan Aruch of Rabbeinu Zalman [HaRav], siman 160, se'if 9.

clarification.explanation: Work disqualifies water for washing the hands only if the water was drawn water (having been drawn into a vessel) — whether it was in a vessel or on the ground — and work was done in it, and it was afterward taken up in a vessel for washing the hands. But if work was done in the water of a mikveh or a spring while it was still attached to the ground, the water was not disqualified for washing the hands. A change of the water's appearance disqualifies it for washing the hands even when the water is attached. All this refers to washing the hands (pouring water over the hands). But if one wishes to immerse the hands in the water, it is permitted to immerse them in water that is valid for immersing the whole body, such as a spring in which a change of appearance does not disqualify, or a mikveh whose water changed appearance due to something without substance (such as the rinsing of baskets of olives and grapes) or into which colored water fell, according to the details in Yoreh De'ah siman 201 and in the Shulchan Aruch of Rabbeinu Zalman, siman 160, se'if 9.
takeaways: Work disqualifies drawn water for washing the hands, but does not disqualify the water of an attached mikveh or spring.
A change of appearance disqualifies water for washing the hands even when it is attached [to the ground].
One may immerse the hands in water valid for immersing the whole body, even if it has certain kinds of change of appearance.

paragraphs: Water in which a baker dipped rolls (gluskin) — even if its appearance did not change — is disqualified. But if he dipped his hands in it and spread [the water] over the surface of the rolls, or took some in his cupped hands, then the water remaining in the vessel had no work done to it, since dipping one's hand in it is not called 'work' unless one rinses hands that are dirty in it; therefore this water remains valid for washing the hands. But if he rinsed dough stuck to his hands in it, it is disqualified even though its appearance did not change. And even though some disagree and hold that rinsing the hands is not considered 'work' that disqualifies the water for washing the hands, since he also wants to wash his hands with it now — nevertheless, the first opinion is the primary one, and it is disqualified for washing the hands, as mentioned by the later authorities.

clarification.explanation: Water in which a baker dipped rolls, even if the water's color did not change, is disqualified for washing the hands, because 'work' (use for another purpose) was done with it, which disqualifies it. But if he only dipped his hands in the water and spread it over the surface of a roll, or took some of it in his cupped hands, this is not 'work' that disqualifies, as long as his hands were not dirty and he merely dipped them in clean water (not a rinsing-away of dirt). Therefore the water remaining in the vessel in this case is still valid for washing the hands. But if he rinsed his hands in it to remove dough stuck to them, the water is disqualified, even if its appearance did not change, because this is already a 'rinsing labor' and not mere dipping. Some disagree and hold that even rinsing off dough is not considered work that disqualifies (since he also wants to wash his hands in it), but the primary halachah follows the first, stricter opinion.
takeaways: Water used to dip bread/rolls is disqualified for washing due to 'work,' even without a change of appearance.
Water in which only clean hands (without dirt) were dipped remains valid; water used to rinse dough stuck to the hands is disqualified.

paragraphs: Water that stands before a barber — if its appearance changed, it is disqualified; if not, it is valid. For when the barber dips [his hands] in it to moisten the hair, this is comparable to dipping one's hand and spreading it on the surface of a roll, where the water that remains has had no work done to it, as mentioned in the Shulchan Aruch of Rabbeinu Zalman, se'if 7.

clarification.explanation: Water that stood before the barber — if its appearance changed, it was disqualified for use. But if its appearance did not change, it is valid. The reason is that the barber dips his hands in the water to moisten the hair, and this action is comparable to a person who dips his hand and spreads it over the surface of a loaf of bread — the water remaining in the vessel is not considered water that had work done to it, and therefore is not disqualified.
takeaways: If the water's appearance changed, the water is disqualified.
If the water's appearance did not change, the water is valid, because dipping the hand to moisten hair is not considered 'work' that disqualifies the water.

paragraphs: If one cooled a vessel containing wine or beer or the like in water, that water is disqualified for washing the hands, since this is considered 'work' having been done in it. However, if the wine or beer was already cold and he placed it in the water only to preserve its coolness so that it would not warm up, the water remains valid. Therefore, the practice here in our city in the summer of taking wine or beer out of the cellar, which is cold from the cellar's own coolness, and merely placing it in a vessel of water near the table to preserve its coolness so that it does not warm from the heat of the air — the water in that vessel is valid for washing the hands.

clarification.explanation: If one cooled a vessel containing wine, beer, or the like in water, the water is disqualified for washing the hands, since this is considered that 'work' (use for cooling) was done with it. But if the wine or beer was already cold, and it was placed in the water only to preserve its existing coolness (and not to cool it anew), the water remains valid. Therefore, the widespread custom in Baghdad in the summer months of taking wine or beer out of the cool cellar and placing it in a vessel of water beside the table only so that it maintains its existing coolness and does not warm from the heat of the air — the water in that vessel is valid for washing the hands.
takeaways: Water used for active cooling (reducing heat) of wine/beer is disqualified due to 'work.'
Water used only to preserve existing coolness (not to actively cool) remains valid for washing.

paragraphs: If one put roses or myrtle in the water so that they would not wilt, this is considered that work was done in it, and it is disqualified for washing the hands. This is not comparable to the wine and beer mentioned above, for here it is different, since myrtle and roses that were in the air without water must have become somewhat dry, and when placed in water they cannot but improve, as mentioned by the later authorities.

clarification.explanation: If one places flowers such as roses or myrtle branches in water so that they will not wilt and will stay fresh, it is considered that 'work' was done with the water, and it is therefore disqualified for washing the hands. This differs from the wine or beer mentioned earlier, because flowers and branches that were in the air without water inevitably become somewhat dry, and when placed in water they cannot but improve and be revived.
takeaways: Water in which roses or myrtle were placed so they would not wilt is disqualified for washing the hands.

paragraphs: If one filled a vessel with water so that its holes and cracks would be sealed, and likewise water in which iron was quenched, and likewise if one placed water in a vessel that has measurement marks and puts meat or the like into it, and the water rises to the marks, and thereby he knows the weight of the meat — this is considered that work was done in it, and it is disqualified, as mentioned by the later authorities.

clarification.explanation: Water that a person filled into a vessel in order to seal holes and cracks in the vessel, and likewise water used to quench hot iron (tempering), and likewise water placed in a vessel with measurement marks (se'if lines) in order to weigh meat by it (measuring by the rise in water level) — all of these are considered to be water in which 'work' was done, and are therefore disqualified for washing the hands.
takeaways: Water used to seal holes, to quench iron, or to measure weight (via a vessel's markings) is disqualified for washing, since work was done with it.

paragraphs: It is the practice of those who make beer or rosewater to place a barrel full of water next to the pot on the fire containing the dates or roses, and to place a copper vessel within the water in the barrel, and to bring two reeds fashioned like a bow, fitting one end onto the lid of the pot and the other end onto the mouth of that copper vessel, so that the vapor passes through the reeds and falls into the copper vessel. Now, that water in the barrel in which the copper vessel is placed is considered to have had work done in it, and is disqualified for washing the hands, as mentioned by the later authorities.

clarification.explanation: In the process of making beer or rosewater, it is customary to place a barrel full of water next to the pot on the fire (in which dates or roses are cooking), and to place a copper vessel within the water of the barrel. Two reeds shaped like an arc are connected — one end to the lid of the pot and the other end to the mouth of the copper vessel — so that the cooking vapor (steam) passes through the reeds and drips into the copper vessel. Since the water in the barrel serves to cool [the vessel] (cooling the copper vessel and aiding the condensation of the vapor), it is considered to have had work done in it, and is therefore disqualified for washing the hands.
takeaways: Water used in a distillation/condensation process (such as cooling a vessel to condense vapor when making beer) is disqualified for washing due to work.

paragraphs: If one filled vessels with water so that the vessels would become saturated with water and not absorb wine or oil that would be put into them afterward, this water too is disqualified for washing the hands, since work was done in it. The same rule applies if one put water in a vessel to know whether it is punctured or not — that water is disqualified. Likewise, leather water-vessels called in Arabic matarah (water-skin for travel), or dolka (a bathing jug), or qirbi (a water-skin), which are water vessels whose usual custom, before their principal use, is to have water placed in them for several days, changing the water each day until the bitter taste [of the leather] departs — this water has had 'work' done in it and is disqualified, and a person should understand from his own reasoning any similar case.

clarification.explanation: Water used to fill a vessel so that the vessel would become saturated with water and not absorb wine or oil that would later be put into it is disqualified for washing the hands, since work was done with it. Likewise, water placed in a vessel merely to check whether the vessel is punctured is also disqualified. And likewise, leather vessels intended for water ('matarah' — water for travel, 'dolka' — a bathing jug, 'qirbi' — a waterskin), whose custom is to first be used for several days, changing the water daily until the initial bitter taste departs — this water is considered to have had 'work' done to it (the curing of the vessel), and is disqualified for washing; and a person should understand from his own reasoning how to identify similar cases.
takeaways: Water used to saturate a vessel (so it won't absorb wine/oil), to check for holes, or to cure a new leather vessel of its initial bitterness — all are disqualified for washing due to work.

paragraphs: If a dog, cat, or pig drank from the water, it is disqualified lechatchilah [ab initio], since [such water] becomes repugnant and is considered like waste water, but after the fact Maran permitted it. However, if other animals, beasts, or fowl drank from it, it is not disqualified even lechatchilah. Some hold that it is disqualified if chickens drank from it, and the same applies to other fowl, except for doves, and it is good to be concerned for this lechatchilah. Therefore, every person should warn the members of his household to always cover the water that they prepare for washing the hands. And this disqualification lechatchilah applies specifically to drawn water; but a spring or mikveh is not disqualified even lechatchilah if those [animals] mentioned drank from it — there is no concern at all in that case.

clarification.explanation: If a dog, cat, or pig drank from the water, it is disqualified lechatchilah for washing the hands, because it is considered repugnant and akin to waste water; but after the fact (if one has already washed with it), Maran permitted it. If other livestock, wild animals, or fowl drank from the water, it is not disqualified even lechatchilah. Some also disqualify it if chickens drank from it (and the same applies to other fowl, except doves), and it is proper to be concerned about this lechatchilah. Therefore, one should warn the members of his household to always cover water intended for washing the hands. Important: all this disqualification applies only to drawn water (water drawn into a vessel); but the water of a spring or mikveh is never disqualified, even lechatchilah, even if these animals drank from it — there is no concern at all in that case.
takeaways: Drawn water that a dog/cat/pig drank from is disqualified lechatchilah (though valid after the fact); it is proper to always keep washing-water covered.
The water of a spring or mikveh is never disqualified by animals drinking from it, even lechatchilah.

paragraphs: Water that was brought into the outhouse for wiping is disqualified for washing the hands, since it is repugnant. Likewise, salty, foul-smelling, or bitter water is disqualified, since a dog cannot drink from it. But the water of the wells found here in our city is valid for washing the hands, since it is not overly salty and a dog does drink from it. The hot springs of Tiberias, which are bitter, are disqualified for washing the hands; however, if there are forty se'ah in one place, one may immerse his hands in them, for then his hands become valid through immersion. Seawater is exceedingly salty and unfit even for a dog, and is therefore disqualified unless it was boiled, in which case it becomes fit. And one who travels by ship on the sea and has no proper water and cannot boil any — what should he do? He should bring a perforated vessel and fill it from the sea, and stand at the ship's edge, and wash his hands from that vessel into the sea, since a connecting stream (nitzok) constitutes a connection; and since the vessel is perforated, it drains water into the sea, and when he washes from it, it is as though he immersed his hands in the sea itself. But this should be done only in a case of pressing need, since some disagree and hold that this [nitzok] does not constitute a [halachic] connection; and if he must resort to this, he should not recite the berachah with God's name and kingship, but should have the name and kingship in mind in his heart.

clarification.explanation: Water brought into the outhouse for cleansing purposes is disqualified for washing the hands, since it is repugnant. Likewise, salty, foul-smelling, or bitter water is disqualified, since even a dog cannot drink from it. But the water of the wells found in Baghdad is valid for washing the hands, since it is not overly salty and a dog can drink from it. The hot springs of Tiberias, being bitter, are disqualified for washing the hands — unless there are forty se'ah in one place, in which case one may immerse (not pour-wash) his hands in them, and they become valid by immersion. Seawater is exceedingly salty and unfit even for a dog, and is therefore disqualified unless it was boiled. One who finds himself on a ship at sea without valid water and unable to boil any: he should bring a perforated vessel, fill it from the sea, and stand at the edge of the ship and wash his hands from within that vessel into the sea — because a perforated vessel that drains its contents into the sea forms a 'connection' (nitzok chibur) between the water in the vessel and the sea, as though he had immersed his hands directly in the sea. But this is permitted only in a case of pressing need, since some disagree and hold that a connecting stream (nitzok) is not a true [halachic] connection — and in such a case he should not recite the berachah aloud, but should have it in mind in his heart.
takeaways: Water from an outhouse, or that is salty, foul-smelling, or bitter, is disqualified; ordinary well water in Baghdad is valid.
On a ship at sea without valid water, one may use a perforated vessel that drains into the sea (nitzok chibur) as a last resort, without reciting the berachah aloud.

paragraphs: If one washed his hands and afterward some doubt arose as to whether that water was disqualified — even though a doubt in a rabbinic matter is resolved leniently — nevertheless, if he has other water that is certainly valid, he should wash again to remove the doubt, but should not recite the berachah a second time.

clarification.explanation: If a person washed his hands, and afterward a doubt arose as to whether the water he had washed with was disqualified — even though a doubt in a rabbinic law is resolved leniently — nevertheless, if he has other water that is certainly valid, he must wash his hands again in order to remove the doubt, but he should not recite the berachah again on this second washing.
takeaways: A doubt about the validity of washing water: if other certainly-valid water is available, one should wash again (without a further berachah), even though a rabbinic doubt is normally resolved leniently.

paragraphs: If, after having recited the berachah of HaMotzi, he learned that the water was disqualified, he should eat less than a kezayit [an olive's bulk], and then wash again with valid water and finish his meal. If he had, in the meantime, turned his attention away from the meal or interrupted it with speech, he should wash his hands again and recite the berachah on washing the hands. But if he did not interrupt with unrelated speech and did not turn his attention away, he should not recite the berachah again.

clarification.explanation: If, after already reciting the berachah of HaMotzi (the blessing over bread), he learns that the water with which he washed was disqualified, he should eat a bit less than a kezayit of the bread (so as not to have recited the HaMotzi in vain), and then wash his hands again with valid water and continue his meal. If in the meantime he turned his attention away from the meal or interrupted with speech (unrelated to the meal), he must wash his hands again and also recite the berachah on the new washing; but if he did not interrupt with outside speech and did not turn his attention away, he should not recite the berachah again on the washing.
takeaways: Discovering that the washing water was disqualified after the HaMotzi blessing: eat a little (less than a kezayit), wash again with valid water, and continue — a repeated berachah on the washing is required only if the meal was interrupted by speech or a distraction of attention.

paragraphs: If one took a piece of snow in his hand and rubbed his hands with it, this does not constitute a valid washing. But if there is forty se'ah of snow within a pit, it is permitted to immerse one's hands in it, and it is valid by the law of immersion. Some permit this even if the snow is not within a pit but is spread over the surface of the ground, provided in any case that there is forty se'ah of it, and one thrusts his hands into it. Some disagree and hold that immersion does not avail for the hands in snow at all; therefore one should not rely on immersion in snow except in a case of pressing need where there is no other remedy available. And if the snow was melted and turned into water, then one may wash his hands from it, or immerse them if there are forty se'ah, according to all opinions.

clarification.explanation: If one took a piece of snow in his hand and rubbed his hands with it, this is not considered a valid washing. But if there is a quantity of snow amounting to forty se'ah within a pit, it is permitted to immerse the hands in it, and this is valid by the law of immersion. Some permit this even if the snow is not in a pit but spread over the surface of the ground, provided there is a measure of forty se'ah and one thrusts the hands into it. Some disagree and hold that immersion in snow does not avail for the hands at all, and therefore one should not rely on immersion in snow except in a case of pressing need when there is no other solution. If the snow was crushed and turned into actual water, then one may wash the hands from it as usual, or immerse them if there is a measure of forty se'ah — and this is valid according to all opinions.
takeaways: Snow measuring forty se'ah (in a pit or spread out) is suitable for immersing the hands in a case of pressing need; merely rubbing with a piece of snow does not constitute a valid washing at all.
If the snow melted into water, it is fully valid for washing or immersion as usual, according to all opinions.

paragraphs: Water so hot that the hand recoils from it — that is, water hot enough to scald a baby's belly — even though Maran permits washing with it, one should be concerned for the stricter opinion and not wash until it cools from such heat; but in a case of pressing need where he cannot wait, it is permitted to wash with it, only he should not recite the berachah with God's name and kingship, but should have the name and kingship in mind in his heart at the time of the berachah. Therefore, elderly people who are accustomed to washing in hot water in the winter should be careful that the water is only lukewarm, and not as hot as would scald a baby's belly.

clarification.explanation: Water so hot that the hand recoils from it (i.e., the hand shrinks back from the intense heat) — although Maran permits washing the hands with it, one should be concerned for the stricter opinion and not wash with it until it cools from that degree of heat. In a case of pressing need, when one cannot wait, it is nonetheless permitted to wash with it, but one should not recite the berachah with God's name and kingship — rather, he should say the berachah without the name and kingship, and have them in mind in his heart at the time of the berachah. Therefore, elderly people who are accustomed to washing in hot water in the winter must be careful that the water be only lukewarm and not so hot as to cause a scald.
takeaways: Water that is too hot (scalding) is best avoided for washing, using only lukewarm water instead; in a pressing need one may be lenient, but should recite the berachah without God's name and kingship, having it in mind in the heart.

paragraphs: Some say that only water, and no other liquid, is valid for washing the hands; but in a case of pressing need, when water is unavailable, it is permitted with other liquids, only one should not recite the berachah but should have it in mind in his heart, as mentioned above.

clarification.explanation: Some hold that washing the hands is valid only with water and not with other liquids. In a case of pressing need, when there is no possibility of obtaining water, it is permitted to be lenient and use other liquids for washing, but one should not recite the berachah aloud, but rather have the berachah in mind in his heart, as explained above in similar cases.
takeaways: Water is the basic requirement for washing the hands; only in a case of pressing need may one be lenient with other liquids, and without a spoken berachah.

paragraphs: Valid water into which a small amount of disqualified water was put — the disqualified water is nullified in the majority, even if the disqualified water reaches the measure of a revi'it, and one may nullify it lechatchilah [ab initio, deliberately].

clarification.explanation: If a small amount of disqualified water is added to a larger quantity of valid water, the disqualified water is nullified by the majority (the larger quantity of valid water nullifies the small disqualified amount) — even if the disqualified water alone reaches the measure of a revi'it. And one may nullify it in this way even lechatchilah (deliberately).
takeaways: A small amount of disqualified water mixed into a large amount of valid water is nullified by the majority, even if the disqualified water alone reaches a revi'it, and this is permitted even lechatchilah.

paragraphs: It is written in Chayei Adam, klal 40, ot 20, that one who touches, in the middle of a meal, a Torah scroll, tefillin, their straps, or a scroll written on parchment according to halachah, must wash his hands but should not recite the berachah — see there. And in the holy work Rav Pe'alim I was asked about this, and I wrote that the Gaon [author of] Panim Me'irot, part 1, siman 15, addressed this matter and gave a sufficient reason that washing is not required at all, differing from Chayei Adam — and his words are clear.

clarification.explanation: It is written in the book Chayei Adam that one who touches, in the middle of a meal, a Torah scroll, tefillin, their straps, or a scroll properly written on parchment, must wash his hands, but without a berachah. However, Rabbi Yosef Chaim was asked about this and cites the view of the Gaon Panim Me'irot, who wrote a convincing reason that no washing at all is required in such a case, contrary to the view of Chayei Adam — and Rabbi Yosef Chaim concludes that the words of the Panim Me'irot are correct as halachah.
takeaways: One who touches a Torah scroll, tefillin, or holy parchment in the middle of a meal is not obligated to wash his hands, following the view of the Panim Me'irot (against the stricter view of the Chayei Adam).

paragraphs: One who touched, in the middle of a meal, his thigh or leg or other covered parts of the body, or scratched his head, must wash his hands but should not recite the berachah on washing the hands. But if he touched the hair of his head without scratching it, no washing is required. And if he touched a soiled place with one hand only, he need wash only that hand — and even for eating fruit or drinking water alone, if he knows that his hands touched a soiled place, he should wash for the sake of the berachah.

clarification.explanation: One who, in the middle of a meal, touched his thigh or leg (a leg part), or other bodily parts normally covered (private areas), or scratched his head, is obligated to wash his hands, but without a berachah. But if he merely touched the hair of his head without scratching it, no washing at all is required. If he touched a soiled place with only one hand, he need wash only that hand. Even when it comes to eating fruit or drinking water alone (which do not fundamentally require washing), if he knows that his hand touched a soiled place, he should wash for the sake of the berachah [that he must recite over the food] (since one may not recite a berachah with unclean hands).
takeaways: Touching a covered/soiled part of the body during a meal requires washing (without a berachah); scratching the hair of the head requires washing, merely touching the hair without scratching does not.
If only one hand touched a soiled place, it suffices to wash only that hand.

paragraphs: One who dozes off in the middle of a meal for less time than sixty breaths does not need to wash his hands; but for longer, he must wash his hands, even during the day. However, he need not recite the berachah on washing the hands, even if he was overcome by sleep for as long as about an hour or more.

clarification.explanation: One who dozed off in the middle of a meal for less than sixty breaths (a short time) is not obligated to wash his hands again. If he fell asleep longer than that, he must wash his hands again, even if this occurs during the day (not only night sleep). Nevertheless, he need not recite a berachah on this washing, even if he was overcome by a long sleep of about an hour or more.
takeaways: A brief doze (less than sixty breaths) in the middle of a meal does not require re-washing; a longer sleep requires washing, but without a berachah.

paragraphs: One who prays in the middle of a meal — some say he must wash his hands, and some say he need not. Therefore, if he has water, he should wash his hands to be concerned for the stricter view, but should not recite the berachah; and if he has no water, he may rely on the lenient view — see Chayei Adam and Chesed LaAlafim.

clarification.explanation: One who recites a prayer (such as Minchah) in the middle of his meal — the halachic authorities disagree as to whether he must wash his hands again before praying: some say he must, some say he need not. Therefore, in practice: if water is readily available, he should wash his hands to be concerned for the stricter opinion, but should not recite the berachah on the washing (since according to the lenient view no washing is required, and in a doubt about berachot we are lenient). And if he has no water, he may rely on the lenient view and pray without washing. (See Chayei Adam and Chesed LaAlafim.)
takeaways: If water is available, wash without a berachah, out of concern for the stricter view.
If no water is available, rely on the lenient view and pray without washing.

paragraphs: Anything that constitutes a chatzitzah [interposition] for immersion constitutes a chatzitzah for washing the hands — such as dirt beneath the fingernail in the place where the nail extends beyond the flesh, and dough beneath the nail even opposite the flesh itself. Therefore a person should not grow his nails long, so as not to come to a stumbling block in washing the hands through interposition. And apart from this, growing the nails long is harsh and bitter for a person's soul, and causes an increase and nourishment for the external [evil] forces, as will be explained elsewhere, please God. And a mourner, within the thirty days [of mourning], should stand guard to clean them every day. But on Shabbat it is forbidden to scrape out the dirt beneath the fingernail, since in removing the dirt from beneath it one smooths the nail [an act forbidden on Shabbat]; rather, he should wash them with water. And a bandage on a person's flesh that he cannot remove before washing because of the wound — I have already written above in Parashat Shemini (ot 14) that one need not wash the place under the bandage, see there. And a nail that has partly detached, one should cut it off, since it constitutes an interposition once it has partly detached.

clarification.explanation: Anything that constitutes an interposition (chatzitzah, separating between the water and the skin, and thereby invalidating) for immersion also constitutes an interposition for washing the hands. For example: dirt (soil) beneath the fingernail in the place where the nail extends beyond the flesh of the finger, and likewise dough beneath the nail — these interpose even when they are exactly opposite the flesh. Therefore a person should refrain from growing his nails excessively, so as not to stumble into an interposition in washing the hands. Beyond this, growing the nails excessively is also harsh and bitter for a person's soul and strengthens the forces of impurity ('external forces'), as will be explained elsewhere. However, a person in mourning (within thirty days of the death of a relative) is obligated to stand guard and clean his nails every day (even though a mourner does not cut his nails during this period, he is obligated to keep them clean of dirt). On Shabbat it is forbidden to scrape out the dirt beneath the fingernail, because doing so 'smooths' the nail — a forbidden labor on Shabbat; rather, one should simply wash the hands with water. A bandage on a person's flesh that cannot be removed before washing because of the wound underneath — as explained above in Parashat Shemini, one need not wash the area under the bandage itself. A fingernail of which part has become detached should be cut off, since it constitutes an interposition from the moment it has become even partly detached.
takeaways: Dirt beneath the fingernail (especially beyond the flesh) constitutes an interposition for washing — therefore one should avoid growing long nails and should keep them clean, even during mourning.

On Shabbat it is forbidden to scrape dirt from beneath the fingernail (a forbidden 'smoothing' labor) — only washing with water is permitted; a nail that has partly detached should be cut off, since it constitutes an interposition.

paragraphs: Ink and dye, if wet, do not constitute an interposition, since they are dissolved by the water; but when dry, they constitute an interposition if there is substance to them on the hands. However, the mere appearance of the color does not constitute an interposition, since there is no substance at all to it. And one whose trade is dyeing — the dye does not constitute an interposition for him even if there is substance of it on his hands; and likewise a scribe whose hands are soiled with ink, since he is accustomed to this, it does not constitute an interposition. But a person whose trade is not this — if there is substance of ink on his hands, it constitutes an interposition. And every person must pay attention to this, since it is common and frequent among people that their hands become soiled from writing, with actual substance of ink on their hands. Likewise a shochet [ritual slaughterer] and a butcher, whose trade involves their hands habitually being soiled with blood, this does not constitute an interposition for them, even though there is substance to the blood.

clarification.explanation: Ink and dye, if wet, do not constitute an interposition in washing, since they dissolve and are washed away by the water. But when dry, they constitute an interposition if there is 'substance' (actual thickness/mass) to them on the hands; but if only a tint of the color remains without any actual substance, this does not constitute an interposition. One whose trade is dyeing — the dye does not constitute an interposition for him at all, even if there is substance on his hands, and likewise a scribe whose hands are soiled with ink — since he is accustomed and habituated to this, it does not constitute an interposition. But a person whose trade is not this — if there is substance of ink on his hands, it does constitute an interposition, and therefore every person should pay attention to this, since it is common for hands to become soiled from writing. Likewise, a shochet and a butcher, whose trade causes their hands to always be soiled with blood, this does not constitute an interposition for them, even though there is substance of blood [on their hands].
takeaways: Dry ink or dye with actual substance constitutes an interposition for washing (unless it is merely a tint without thickness), but for tradespeople habituated to it (a dyer, a scribe, a shochet, a butcher) it does not constitute an interposition.

paragraphs: A ring that has a precious stone in it — such as what is called almas (a white stone/diamond), or zamrud (turquoise-blue colored), or yaqut (red colored), or piruza (a precious stone), and the like — must be removed at the time of washing, and merely loosening it does not avail, even if it is loose; one should remove it entirely, since we are not expert in determining exactly how loose is 'loose enough.' After the fact, if it was loose, the washing is valid; but if it was tight, the washing is not valid. And if it has no precious stone, for men — who are not accustomed to kneading dough — one may rely on the lenient view and not remove it. But for women, who are accustomed to kneading and are particular to remove it at the time of kneading, since it is difficult for them to knead with the ring still on their hand, they must remove it. And even for men, removing it will bring a blessing upon him.

clarification.explanation: A ring that has a precious stone in it — such as a diamond ('almas'), a turquoise-blue stone ('zamrud'), a red stone ('yaqut'), or a 'piruza' — must be removed at the time of washing the hands, and mere loosening does not suffice, even if it is loose; rather one must remove it entirely, since we are not expert enough to know precisely how 'loose' is loose enough for the water to pass beneath it. After the fact, if the ring was loose, the washing is valid even without removing it; but if it was tight, the washing is not valid. A ring without a precious stone — for men, who are not accustomed to kneading dough, one may rely on the lenient opinions and not remove it. But for women, who are accustomed to kneading dough and are particular to remove rings at the time of kneading because it is difficult to knead with the ring on the hand, must remove it at the time of washing as well. Even for men, one who removes the ring for washing — a blessing will come upon him (it is proper to do so, even though not obligatory).
takeaways: A ring with a precious stone must be entirely removed at washing (not merely loosened), otherwise the washing may be invalid if the ring was tight.
A ring without a stone: men are not obligated to remove it; women (due to their habit of removing it for kneading) must remove it.
